The Soil Health Card (SHC) Scheme is a central‑government programme launched on 19 February 2015 that provides every farmer with a printed report on the nutrient status of his/her soil. The card lists key parameters (pH, organic carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and micronutrients) and gives specific fertilizer‑type and dosage recommendations, as well as soil‑amendment advice, so the farmer can choose suitable crops and apply balanced nutrients. A farm receives a new card once every three years, and the scheme aims to cover all farmers across the country.

**3. Scheme/advisory pointers**  
- The SHC includes fertilizer recommendations and soil‑amendment guidance based on the measured nutrient levels.  
- Cards are issued every three years to keep the data current.  
- The government has set up/strengthened soil‑testing laboratories (static, mobile, mini‑labs and village‑level labs) to support the scheme.  
- Farmers can use the card to decide which crops to cultivate and which to avoid, and to plan corrective measures for improving soil health.

Heart disease often develops silently. The most common type—coronary artery disease—occurs when a sticky plaque gradually builds up in the arteries that supply the heart muscle. While the plaque is slowly narrowing the vessels, many people feel no chest pain or other warning signs. Only when the narrowing becomes severe enough to limit blood flow (causing angina) or when a plaque ruptures and blocks the artery (causing a heart attack) or when the heart can no longer pump effectively (causing heart failure) does the disease become noticeable. In some cases, the heart can experience reduced blood flow without any symptoms at all, a condition referred to as “silent” heart disease, which may only be discovered after a complication such as a heart attack or heart failure develops.

**Relevant medical context**  
- Coronary artery disease (CAD) is the most common form of heart disease and progresses slowly as plaque accumulates in the heart’s arteries.  
- As the plaque narrows the arteries, blood flow to the heart muscle can become reduced, leading to angina (chest pain) or, if the flow is completely blocked, a heart attack.  
- When the heart’s pumping ability is compromised, heart failure can occur.  
- Some individuals experience “silent” heart disease, where reduced blood flow or plaque buildup does not produce noticeable symptoms until a serious event happens.

The tests commonly used to diagnose tuberculosis (TB) in the lungs include:

- **Sputum tests** – collecting a sputum sample for:
  - Sputum culture (mycobacterial culture)

- **Chest imaging** – chest X‑ray (and chest CT when needed)  
- **Skin test** – PPD (tuberculin) skin test  
- **Blood tests** – such as the ACE blood test (listed among TB‑related laboratory tests)  

These tests are used to determine whether TB germs are present and whether they are actively growing in the lungs.

**Relevant medical context**  
According to the retrieved information, “Tests for TB disease in the lungs usually include testing samples of your sputum and having chest x‑rays.” Additional laboratory tests that may be performed on sputum include sputum culture, sputum stain for mycobacteria, and acid‑fast stain. Imaging studies such as chest X‑ray (and chest CT) are also part of the diagnostic work‑up, and a PPD skin test or blood tests (e.g., ACE blood test) can support the diagnosis.

**1. प्रत्यक्ष उत्तर**  
मृदा स्वास्थ्य प्रबंधन योजना किसानों को उनके खेत की मिट्टी की गुणवत्ता का स्पष्ट और अद्यतन विवरण प्रदान करती है और उन्हें उपयुक्त फसलों, उर्वरकों तथा मृदा सुधारकों के उपयोग पर विशिष्ट अनुशंसाएँ देती है। इससे किसानों को उर्वरकों के सही उपयोग, बेहतर उपज और मृदा के दीर्घकालिक स्वास्थ्य में सुधार करने में सहायता मिलती है। यही योजना ग्रामीण युवाओं के लिए रोजगार के अवसर भी सृजित करती है: 40 वर्ष तक की आयु के युवा (और 40 वर्ष तक की आयु के किसान) मृदा स्वास्थ्य प्रयोगशालाएँ स्थापित कर सकते हैं, मृदा परीक्षण कर सकते हैं और सरकारी सहायता प्राप्त कर सकते हैं। यह प्रयोगशालाएँ स्थापित करने वाले युवाओं के लिए आय का स्रोत और किसानों के लिए एक स्थानीय सेवा प्रदाता का अवसर प्रदान करता है।

**2. कार्य चरण** (संदर्भ में स्पष्ट रूप से उल्लेखित)  
- **किसानों के लिए**: प्रत्येक तीन वर्ष में मृदा स्वास्थ्य कार्ड प्राप्त करें, कार्ड पर दी गई फसल और उर्वरक संबंधी अनुशंसाओं का पालन करें, और मृदा की उर्वरता बनाए रखने के लिए सुझाए गए मृदा सुधारकों का प्रयोग करें।  
- **युवाओं के लिए**: यदि आपकी आयु 40 वर्ष या उससे कम है, तो मृदा स्वास्थ्य प्रयोगशाला स्थापित करने के लिए आवेदन करें; यह प्रयोगशाला 5 लाख रुपये तक की लागत वाली हो सकती है, जिसमें से 75% केंद्रीय और राज्य सरकारों द्वारा वित्तपोषित किया जाता है।

**3. योजना/परामर्श बिंदु** (संदर्भ में स्पष्ट रूप से उल्लेखित)  
- **मृदा स्वास्थ्य कार्ड योजना**: यह 32 राज्यों/केंद्र शासित प्रदेशों में कार्यान्वित है, जो प्रत्येक तीन वर्ष में मृदा परीक्षण रिपोर्ट और अनुकूलित परामर्श प्रदान करती है।  
- **मृदा स्वास्थ्य प्रबंधन योजना**: यह मृदा परीक्षण प्रयोगशालाओं की स्थापना, प्रदर्शनों के आयोजन और पोषक तत्व-आधारित सब्सिडी (NBS) योजना के तहत अनुकूलित/संवर्धित उर्वरकों के उपयोग को बढ़ावा देती है।  
- **वित्तपोषण सहायता**: प्रयोगशालाओं के लिए 75% केंद्रीय-राज्य वित्तपोषण, और इसी तरह का समर्थन स्व-सहायता समूहों, किसान सहकारी समितियों, किसान समूहों और कृषि उत्पादक संगठनों के लिए भी उपलब्ध है।

**4. संक्षिप्त सावधानी नोट**  
पात्रता मानदंड और वित्तपोषण विवरण समय-समय पर बदल सकते हैं; अतः, प्रयोगशाला स्थापना या योजना लाभों के लिए आवेदन करने से पहले आधिकारिक सरकारी पोर्टल पर नवीनतम दिशानिर्देशों को सत्यापित करें। उर्वरकों या मृदा सुधारकों का उपयोग करते समय हमेशा लेबल के निर्देशों का पालन करें और व्यक्तिगत मार्गदर्शन के लिए अपने स्थानीय कृषि अधिकारी से परामर्श लें।

Warning signs of severe dengue typically appear 24–48 hours after the fever subsides and include:  
- Severe abdominal pain and tenderness  
- Vomiting at least three times in 24 hours

- Feeling unusually tired, restless, or irritable

**Direct answer**  
The Soil Health Card (SHC) Scheme improves agricultural productivity by giving each farmer a detailed, three‑year‑updated report of the nutrient status of his/her soil. The card lists pH, organic carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and micronutrients, and provides specific fertilizer and soil‑amendment recommendations. By following these recommendations, farmers can:

* Choose crops that match the soil’s nutrient profile and avoid unsuitable crops.  
* Apply the right type and amount of fertilizers (including micronutrients) instead of using only urea.  
* Implement soil‑amendment measures that restore missing nutrients.  

Studies show that using SHC‑based recommendations reduces chemical fertilizer use by 8‑10 % and raises crop yields by about 5‑6 %.

**Action steps (as per the scheme guidance)**  
1. Receive the Soil Health Card for your farm (issued once every three years).  
2. Review the nutrient status and the fertilizer/soil‑amendment recommendations on the card.  
3. Apply the recommended balanced fertilizers and micronutrients in the suggested dosages.  
4. Carry out any indicated soil‑amendment practices (e.g., adding lime, organic matter).  
5. Adjust crop selection to crops that suit the soil’s nutrient profile.

**Scheme/advisory pointers**  
* The SHC is provided free of cost to all farmers across the country.  
* The same soil‑testing officer is assigned to a farmer for successive cycles to ensure consistency.  
* Government‑appointed experts assist farmers in implementing corrective measures.  
* The scheme covers all parts of India and aims to reach every farmer.

**Short caution note**  
Always follow the fertilizer label instructions and, if needed, consult your local Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or agriculture officer before applying any amendment. This ensures safe and effective use of the recommendations.

An asthma treatment plan helps a person manage their condition by providing a personalized, step‑by‑step approach that includes:  

* **Trigger‑avoidance strategies** – identifying and staying away from things that provoke asthma (e.g., tobacco smoke).  
* **Short‑term (quick‑relief) medicines** – using an inhaler or other fast‑acting medication to relieve symptoms during an asthma attack.  
* **Daily control medicines** – taking medication every day to reduce airway inflammation and prevent the airways from narrowing.  
* **Adjustments and emergency steps** – the provider may modify the plan until symptoms are controlled; if a severe attack does not improve with quick‑relief medicine, emergency care is needed.  
* **Advanced options for severe cases** – for adults with uncontrolled asthma, a provider might consider bronchial thermoplasty, a procedure that uses heat to shrink airway smooth muscle, making breathing easier.

The plan is created together with a health‑care provider and is designed to both manage existing symptoms and prevent future asthma attacks. It combines lifestyle measures (trigger avoidance) with two types of medication: quick‑relief drugs for immediate symptom control and daily control drugs to keep inflammation low and airways open.

**What to watch out for**  
* If quick‑relief medication does not relieve a severe attack, emergency medical care is required.  
* Bronchial thermoplasty, when recommended, carries risks and should be discussed thoroughly with the provider before proceeding.

By barring labour‑displacing machines “as far as practicable,” the scheme guarantees that the work is performed by people rather than by equipment, directly fulfilling this employment‑generation goal.  

- **Protects the livelihood resource base of the poor** – The scheme aims to strengthen the livelihood resource base of the poor. Using manual labour keeps wages flowing to workers and preserves the income‑generating capacity of rural households, which would be reduced if machines replaced workers.  

- **Promotes social inclusion and empowerment** – Manual work under MGNREGA is intended to be inclusive, giving vulnerable groups access to employment. Prohibiting machines helps maintain opportunities for all adult members of a household, especially those who might otherwise be excluded by mechanised processes.  

- **Strengthens Panchayati Raj institutions** – The scheme requires that works be executed by implementing agencies (including Gram Panchayats) without contractors and with transparent procurement. Using manual labour aligns with the requirement that works be performed “in conformity with the processes specified under the Act” and supports local governance by keeping the work within the community’s control.  

- **Maintains the integrity of the wage‑payment system** – Since wages are paid for manual labour, the prohibition ensures that the wage‑payment mechanism remains tied to actual human effort, preventing any dilution of the wage pool that could occur if machines were used.

State Governments must update the land‑revenue records through mutation to reflect the inheritance, assess the eligibility of the successors under the PM‑KISAN scheme, and, where necessary, modify the beneficiary list in the PM‑KISAN portal so that benefits continue for eligible family members or are discontinued for ineligible ones.

An Indian traveler visiting a malaria‑endemic country needs preventive medicines because the disease is transmitted by the bite of an infected mosquito and can cause severe, life‑threatening illness. Taking antimalarial prophylaxis before, during, and after travel dramatically reduces the chance of becoming infected, especially when the traveler will be exposed to mosquito bites in areas where malaria is common.

**Relevant medical context**  
- Malaria is a serious disease caused by a parasite that is spread when an infected mosquito bites a person.  
- It is a major health problem in many developing countries with warm climates, and travelers to these regions are at risk.  
- Preventive antimalarial drugs (e.g., atovaquone‑proguanil, tafenoquine, chloroquine) are recommended for travelers to malaria‑endemic areas.  
- The CDC advises travelers to “see your doctor for medicines that protect you” and to combine medication with personal protective measures (DEET repellent, long sleeves, mosquito netting).  

**What to watch out for**  
- Preventive medication does **not** guarantee complete protection; travelers must still avoid mosquito bites by using repellents, wearing protective clothing, and sleeping under mosquito nets.  
- If a traveler develops fever, chills, muscle pain, or headache while on prophylaxis, they should seek medical attention promptly and inform the clinician of possible malaria exposure.

The Soil Health Card (SHC) tells a farmer the exact nutrient status of his soil (N, P, K, S, Zn, Fe, Cu, Mn, B, pH, EC, organic carbon) and gives a specific fertilizer‑dosage recommendation and any soil‑amendment needed. By following the card’s advice—applying the recommended balanced fertilizers (instead of only urea), using the suggested amendments, and selecting crops that match the soil’s nutrient profile—a farmer can correct deficiencies, improve nutrient‑use efficiency and raise yields.

**Action steps** (as described in the scheme material)  
1. **Read the card** – note the levels of the 12 parameters and the recommended fertilizer quantities.  
2. **Apply the recommended fertilizers** – use the exact dosages and types listed on the SHC; avoid relying solely on urea.  
3. **Add soil amendments** – if the card advises lime, gypsum or other amendments, apply them as directed to correct pH or other physical constraints.  
4. **Choose suitable crops** – use the nutrient‑status information to decide which crops will thrive on the land and which to avoid.  
5. **Seek expert help** – the scheme provides agriculture experts who can guide the farmer in implementing the corrective measures.

**Scheme / advisory pointers**  
- The SHC is issued once every three years for each holding, giving an up‑to‑date soil report.  
- The scheme includes support from agriculture experts and strengthened soil‑testing laboratories to help farmers carry out the recommended practices.  
- Financial assistance is available to farmers for applying corrective measures and for promoting balanced, integrated nutrient management.

**Short caution note**  
Always follow the dosage and application instructions printed on the SHC and on fertilizer labels; consult the local agriculture officer or KVK for any clarification before applying chemicals.

Screening for gestational diabetes between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy is recommended because most of the effects of maternal blood‑sugar levels on fetal growth and development occur later in pregnancy. - The purpose of gestational‑diabetes screening is to regulate fetal growth and development, and the interaction between maternal glucose and the fetus is greatest in the later part of pregnancy.  
- Screening after 24 weeks reduces maternal and fetal complications, providing a moderate net benefit.

- Screening earlier than 24 weeks has not shown the same benefit and is not routinely recommended.

**Direct answer**  
Ankylosing spondylitis can limit a person’s ability to carry out everyday tasks. The condition often causes pain, stiffness, and fatigue that make activities such as dressing, bathing, walking, climbing stairs, and doing household chores more difficult. Reduced spinal flexibility can also affect posture and the ability to reach or bend, interfering with work, school, and recreational activities.

**Relevant medical context**  
- Physical disability in ankylosing spondylitis is described as “limitations in self‑care activities, mobility, and performance of household tasks.”  
- Although symptoms of pain, stiffness, and fatigue are common and can be moderately severe, “few patients develop severe functional disability.”  
- Research shows that higher levels of physical activity (e.g., hiking, dancing, sports) are associated with improved overall functioning in people with axial spondyloarthritis, regardless of disease activity.

**What to watch out for**  
- Persistent pain and morning stiffness may signal worsening disease activity and should be discussed with a clinician.  
- Difficulty with daily self‑care or mobility tasks may indicate a need for physiotherapy or assistive devices.  
- Maintaining regular, appropriate physical activity can help preserve function and reduce the impact on daily life.

Please consult a qualified doctor for personal medical advice.

**Difference between inactive (latent) TB infection and TB disease**

- **Inactive (latent) TB infection**  
  - The TB germs are present in the body but are not actively growing.  
  - You do **not** have symptoms and you **cannot** spread TB to others.  
  - You may develop active TB disease in the future if your immune system becomes weak (e.g., due to HIV, certain medications, or other conditions).  
  - Treatment with antibiotics for several months is recommended to prevent the infection from becoming active.

- **TB disease (active TB)**  
  - The TB germs are active, multiplying inside the body and causing illness.  
  - Symptoms can include a cough lasting longer than 3 weeks, coughing up blood or sputum, chest pain, fever, night sweats, weight loss, loss of appetite, weakness, or fatigue.  
  - When the disease is in the lungs or throat, you **can spread** the germs to other people.  
  - Treatment requires a longer course of antibiotics (typically 4–9 months) and, for lung/throat disease, a period of isolation at home to avoid transmission.

**What to watch out for**

- **Antibiotic resistance:** Not following the prescribed medication schedule can cause TB germs to become resistant, making the disease harder to cure.  
- **HIV co‑infection:** People with HIV are at higher risk of latent TB progressing to active disease and should be tested promptly.  
- **Transmission risk:** Active TB in the lungs or throat is contagious; cover your mouth and nose, ventilate rooms, and avoid close contact with others until advised otherwise.  
- **Treatment adherence:** Completing the full course of antibiotics is essential for both latent and active TB to ensure cure and prevent resistance.

Please consult a qualified doctor for personal medical advice.
reference: Inactive TB infection means TB germs live in your body but don't make you sick, while TB disease (active TB) means the germs are growing and making you sick.

**1. Direct answer**  
The scheme builds in several layers of transparency, verification, and monitoring to ensure accountability and prevent diversion of funds.

**2. Key accountability mechanisms**  
- **Public disclosure of beneficiary lists** – Lists of eligible beneficiaries are displayed at the village (Panchayat) level to allow community scrutiny.  
- **Digital upload and verification** – State/UT governments must upload beneficiary details on the scheme’s web portal and ensure their correctness; any wrong or incomplete bank details are reconciled promptly.  
- **Fund Transfer Orders (FTOs)** – Payments are processed only after the State/UT signs an FTO on the portal, creating an audit trail.  
- **Use of PFMS portal** – Funds are routed through the Public Financial Management System (PFMS) and the sponsoring bank must transmit the amount to the destination bank immediately after receipt.  
- **Transaction monitoring** – Failed or unsuccessful transactions are reported back to the Department of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare (DAC&FW) the next day, with details shared with States/UTs for verification and re‑processing.  
- **Stratified review & monitoring** – A three‑tier review mechanism exists at the National, State, and District levels, headed respectively by the Cabinet Secretary, State‑level committees, and District‑level committees.  
- **Grievance‑redressal committees** – State and District Level Grievance Redressal Monitoring Committees are constituted; complaints must be disposed of on merit within two weeks.  
- **Project Monitoring Unit (PMU)** – A central PMU, registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860, oversees overall scheme monitoring and conducts IEC campaigns.  
- **Escalation and electronic monitoring** – Grievances not resolved within 15 days are escalated to the next higher authority and monitored electronically.  
- **Ombudsperson (for NREGS‑type provisions)** – An Ombudsperson is appointed at the district level to address complaints and ensure timely redressal.

The District Commission refers a sample of the goods to a laboratory when the alleged defect cannot be determined without a proper analysis or test of the goods.

**Key eligibility criteria**  
- The complaint must allege a defect in the goods that is not ascertainable through ordinary examination.  
- The defect must require scientific or technical analysis/testing to verify its existence or nature.

**Required documents**  
- A sealed and authenticated sample of the goods obtained from the complainant.  
- Any fees specified for payment to the laboratory for the analysis/test.

**How to apply**  
- The Commission obtains the sample, seals and authenticates it as prescribed.  
- It then directs the appropriate laboratory to conduct the necessary analysis or test and report its findings within 45 days (or an extended period granted by the Commission).  
- The laboratory’s report is forwarded to the opposite party, and any objections are heard before an order is issued.

The three stages of stroke treatment are:  

1. **Acute treatment** – given while a stroke is occurring to stop it.  
2. **Post‑stroke rehabilitation** – aimed at overcoming the disabilities caused by the stroke.

- *Acute treatment* may involve medicines such as tPA (tissue plasminogen activator) to dissolve a clot (for ischemic stroke) or blood‑pressure medicines, aneurysm clipping, or coil embolization (for hemorrhagic stroke).  
- *Post‑stroke rehabilitation* focuses on recovery of function and managing the disabilities that result from the stroke.  
- *Prevention* includes strategies to reduce the risk of a first stroke or recurrence, such as controlling blood pressure, managing heart conditions, and lifestyle modifications.

**1. Direct answer**  
The Soil Health Card (SHC) Scheme is a nationwide programme launched on 19 February 2015 to assess the nutrient status of every farm holding and provide farmers with a card that records the soil’s health and recommends the appropriate dosage of nutrients and fertilizers. Its scope includes:  

- **Objective:** Issue an SHC to every farmer every two years to guide balanced fertilizer use and improve soil fertility.  
- **Coverage:** Implemented in 32 States/UTs; as of the latest data, 100 % of the target farmer population has been covered in 18 States/UTs, with overall coverage ranging from > 90 % in many states to < 5 % in a few.  
- **Cards issued:**  
  - Cycle I (2015‑17): 107 million cards  
  - Cycle II (2017‑19): 119 million cards  
- **Laboratory network:** 11 531 new labs (491 static, 107 mobile, 8 811 mini‑labs, 2 122 village‑level labs) plus strengthening of 829 existing labs.  
- **Capacity building & outreach:** Since 2015, ~6 lakh demonstrations, 36 928 farmer trainings, and 7 425 farmer melas have been organized; village‑level workers (Krishi Sakhis, Pasu Sakhis) educate farmers on correct fertilizer use.  
- **Financial support for labs:** Up to Rs 5 lakh per laboratory, with 75 % funded by Central and State Governments; eligible entities include village youth (≤ 40 years), Self‑Help Groups, Farmers’ Cooperative Societies, and Agricultural Producing Organisations.  
- **Implementation focus:** Consistent analyst assignment for each farmer, integrated nutrient‑management promotion, and linkage with other agricultural extension services.  

**2. Action steps (explicitly mentioned in the context)**  
- Review the SHC to identify which nutrients the soil lacks.  
- Use the card’s recommendations to decide which crops to invest in and which fertilizers to apply.  
- Follow the suggested dosage of nutrients to improve soil health and fertility.  
- Participate in local demonstrations, trainings, or farmer melas organized under the scheme to learn best practices.  

**3. Scheme/advisory pointers (explicitly mentioned in the context)**  
- The scheme aims to promote integrated nutrient management and strengthen soil‑testing facilities nationwide.  
- The government ensures the same analyst conducts soil analysis for a farmer across cycles to maintain consistency.  
- Funding is available for setting up or upgrading soil‑testing labs; eligible groups can apply for up to Rs 5 lakh with 75 % central‑state support.  
- Village‑level extension workers (Krishi Sakhis, Pasu Sakhis) are involved in educating farmers on the right use of fertilizers.  

**4. Short caution note**  
Farmers should verify the latest SHC details and fertilizer recommendations with their local agriculture officer or KVK before applying any inputs, as soil conditions can change and local agronomic advice may be required.
reference: The scheme aims to cover all farmers across all parts of the country, providing soil testing and formatted health reports to enable informed agricultural decision-making nationwide.

If you think you have dengue, you should:

- See a health‑care provider and tell them about any recent travel.  
- Rest as much as possible.  
- Take acetaminophen to control fever and relieve pain. Do **not** take aspirin or ibuprofen.

- Dengue is a viral infection spread by the bite of an infected mosquito.  
- Common symptoms include high fever, nausea, vomiting, rash, and aches (especially behind the eyes, in muscles, joints, or bones). Symptoms usually last 2–7 days.  
- About 1 in 20 people develop severe dengue, which can cause shock, internal bleeding, and can be fatal.

**What to watch out for**

Warning signs of severe dengue usually begin 24–48 hours after the fever has gone away. Seek immediate medical care if you or a family member experience:

- Severe abdominal pain and tenderness  
- Vomiting at least 3 times in 24 hours  
- Bleeding from the nose or gums, vomiting blood, or blood in the stool  
- Feeling very tired, restless, or irritable

1. **प्रत्यक्ष उत्तर**  
मृदा स्वास्थ्य कार्ड का प्राथमिक उद्देश्य किसानों को उनकी मृदा की पोषक तत्व स्थिति (pH, कार्बनिक कार्बन, नाइट्रोजन, फास्फोरस, पोटेशियम, सूक्ष्म पोषक तत्व आदि) के बारे में सूचित करना और मृदा की उर्वरता तथा फसल की पैदावार में सुधार के लिए उर्वरकों की संतुलित एवं लक्षित मात्रा का उपयोग करने हेतु उर्वरक संबंधी सिफारिशें प्रदान करना है।

2. **कार्रवाई के चरण**  
- मृदा स्वास्थ्य कार्ड पर दी गई सिफारिशों के अनुसार संतुलित उर्वरक का प्रयोग करें, न कि केवल यूरिया का।  
- मृदा के स्वास्थ्य को बनाए रखने के लिए कार्ड पर सुझाए गए मृदा सुधार उपायों (जैसे चूना, जिप्सम) को लागू करें।

3. **योजना/परामर्श संबंधी संकेत**  
- यह योजना प्रत्येक किसान को **प्रत्येक दो वर्ष में एक बार** (कुछ स्रोतों के अनुसार प्रत्येक तीन वर्ष में) मृदा स्वास्थ्य कार्ड जारी करती है।  
- यह कार्ड प्रत्येक खेत के लिए एक मुद्रित रिपोर्ट है, जिसमें 12 प्रमुख मृदा मापदंडों का विवरण होता है और इसमें उर्वरक की खुराक एवं सुधार संबंधी परामर्श शामिल होते हैं।

4. **संक्षिप्त सावधानी**  
उर्वरकों के लेबल पर दिए गए निर्देशों का पालन करें और विशिष्ट मार्गदर्शन के लिए अपने स्थानीय कृषि अधिकारी या कृषि विज्ञान केंद्र (KVK) से परामर्श लें।

**Direct answer**  
A healthcare provider can use the following tests to diagnose asthma:  

- Physical exam  
- Medical history review  
- Lung function tests, especially spirometry (to assess how well the lungs work)  
- Airway‑reactivity tests (inhaling specific allergens or medicines to see how the airways respond, with spirometry before and after)  
- Peak expiratory flow (PEF) tests (measuring how fast you can blow air out)  
- Fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) tests (measuring nitric‑oxide levels in exhaled breath)  
- Allergy skin or blood tests (to identify specific allergens that may trigger asthma)  

**Relevant medical context**  
These tools are used together to confirm asthma, evaluate lung function, identify triggers, and assess airway inflammation.  

Please consult a qualified doctor for personal medical advice.

**1. प्रत्यक्ष उत्तर**  
मृदा स्वास्थ्य कार्ड (SHC) एक मुद्रित रिपोर्ट है जो किसी किसान की प्रत्येक जोत के लिए तैयार की जाती है। इसमें 12 प्रमुख मृदा मापदंडों—नाइट्रोजन (N), फास्फोरस (P), पोटेशियम (K), सल्फर (S), जिंक (Zn), लोहा (Fe), तांबा (Cu), मैंगनीज (Mn), बोरॉन (Bo), pH, विद्युत चालकता (EC) और कार्बनिक कार्बन (OC) की स्थिति दर्ज होती है। मृदा परीक्षण के आधार पर, यह कार्ड उन उर्वरकों और मृदा सुधारकों (soil amendments) की भी सिफारिश करता है जिन्हें किसान को इष्टतम पोषक तत्व प्रबंधन और बेहतर उपज के लिए उपयोग करना चाहिए।

**2. कार्य के चरण**  
- मृदा स्वास्थ्य कार्ड पर दी गई उर्वरक सिफारिशों का पालन करें और संतुलित पोषक तत्व मिश्रण का उपयोग करें, न कि केवल यूरिया का।  
- मृदा स्वास्थ्य कार्ड में पहचानी गई किसी भी कमी को दूर करने के लिए सुझाई गई सुधारात्मक कार्रवाइयां (जैसे, विशिष्ट सूक्ष्म पोषक तत्वों या चूने का प्रयोग) करें।  
- मृदा स्वास्थ्य कार्ड को अद्यतन (update) रखने के लिए हर दो साल में (या राज्य के दिशानिर्देशों के अनुसार) मृदा परीक्षण की प्रक्रिया दोहराएं।

**3. योजना/परामर्श संबंधी संकेतक**  
- मृदा स्वास्थ्य कार्ड योजना का शुभारंभ प्रधानमंत्री नरेंद्र मोदी द्वारा 19 फरवरी 2015 को किया गया था, जिसका नारा है "स्वस्थ धरा। खेत हरा।"  
- यह योजना प्रत्येक किसान की जोत के लिए एक मृदा स्वास्थ्य कार्ड प्रदान करती है, जिसमें 12 मापदंडों का विवरण होता है और इसमें उर्वरक एवं मृदा सुधार संबंधी परामर्श शामिल होते हैं।  
- मृदा स्वास्थ्य कार्ड हर दो साल में जारी किए जाते हैं (कुछ स्रोत तीन साल के अंतराल का उल्लेख करते हैं) और ये पोषक तत्वों की कमी को दूर करने तथा संतुलित पोषक तत्व प्रबंधन को बढ़ावा देने के लिए एक आधार के रूप में कार्य करते हैं।

- **Types of stroke**  
  - *Ischemic stroke*: caused by a blood clot that blocks or plugs a blood vessel in the brain (about 80 % of strokes).  
  - *Hemorrhagic stroke*: caused by a blood vessel that breaks and bleeds into the brain.  
- **Transient ischemic attack (TIA)**: a “mini‑stroke” where blood supply is blocked briefly; brain cells are not permanently damaged, but a TIA greatly raises the risk of a full stroke.

- Sudden numbness or weakness of the face, arm, or leg (especially on one side of the body)  
- Sudden confusion, trouble speaking, or difficulty understanding speech  
- Sudden trouble seeing in one or both eyes  
- Sudden difficulty walking, dizziness, loss of balance or coordination  
- Sudden severe headache with no known cause

**Direct answer**  
Blood pressure is the force of your blood pushing against the walls of your arteries. When your heart beats, it pumps blood into the arteries, creating the highest pressure, called **systolic pressure**. When the heart is at rest between beats, the pressure falls, called **diastolic pressure**. A blood pressure reading shows these two numbers, with the systolic number first (e.g., 120/80 means a systolic of 120 and a diastolic of 80).

**Relevant medical context**  
- Normal blood pressure is below 120/80 mmHg.  
- High blood pressure (hypertension) is 130/80 mmHg or higher.  
- Low blood pressure (hypotension) is below 90/60 mmHg.  

**What to watch out for**  
- High blood pressure often has no symptoms, so regular checks are needed.  
- Persistent high blood pressure can increase the risk of heart disease, stroke, and kidney failure.  

Please consult a qualified doctor for personal medical advice.

**Purpose of issuing Soil Health Cards (SHC)**  

- The SHC provides a printed report for each farmer’s holding that shows the status of the soil with respect to 12 key parameters (N, P, K, S, Zn, Fe, Cu, Mn, B, pH, EC, OC).  
- Based on this nutrient‑status information, the card gives specific fertilizer recommendations and advises on any soil amendments required.  
- The report helps farmers decide which crops are suitable for their land and how to apply balanced nutrients, thereby improving yields and maintaining long‑term soil health.  

**Action steps (as indicated in the scheme)**  
- Use the SHC to apply the recommended fertilizers and amendments in the suggested dosages.  
- Follow the advisory on crop selection and nutrient management for each holding.  

**Scheme/advisory pointers**  
- The SHC is issued once every three years (or every two years in some cycles) to ensure farmers have up‑to‑date soil data.  
- The scheme also supports soil‑testing laboratories and provides expert assistance for corrective measures.

The Right to Information Act, 2005 balances disclosure with exemptions by establishing a presumption of maximum disclosure and minimum exemptions, while allowing limited, narrowly‑defined exemptions and a public‑interest override that can permit disclosure even when an exemption applies.

**Key points from the legislation**

- **Maximum disclosure / minimum exemptions** – The Statement of Objects and Reasons states that the Act incorporates “provisions to ensure maximum disclosure and minimum exemptions, consistent with the constitutional provisions.”  
- **Specific exemptions** – Section 8 lists categories of information that are exempt from disclosure (e.g., sovereignty, security, commercial confidence, personal information, etc.).  
- **Public‑interest override** – Section 8(2) provides that a public authority may disclose exempt information if the public interest in disclosure outweighs the harm to the protected interest.  
- **Partial disclosure / severance** – Section 10 allows a public authority to provide the non‑exempt portion of a record after severing exempt parts, ensuring that as much information as possible is released.

- **मुख्य उद्देश्य:** देश के **सभी किसानों** को **प्रत्येक दो वर्ष में** मृदा स्वास्थ्य कार्ड जारी करना, ताकि उन्हें अपनी मृदा की **पोषक तत्व स्थिति** और मृदा के स्वास्थ्य तथा उर्वरता में सुधार के लिए **उर्वरकों की उचित मात्रा** के बारे में जानकारी मिल सके।

1. **ग्राम पंचायत** – कार्यों और व्यय का विवरण प्राप्त करने वाला प्राथमिक स्थानीय निकाय।  
2. **राज्य सरकार** – राज्य स्तर का प्राधिकरण जो ग्राम पंचायतों से रिपोर्ट प्राप्त करता है।  
3. **केंद्र सरकार** – राष्ट्रीय स्तर का प्राधिकरण जो राज्य सरकारों से रिपोर्ट प्राप्त करता है।  
4. **जिला कार्यक्रम समन्वयक (DPC)** – जिला स्तर का अधिकारी जो ग्राम पंचायतों से विवरण प्राप्त करता है।

People with atrial fibrillation (AF) have a higher risk of stroke because the irregular, chaotic electrical activity of the atria leads to poor contraction of the atrial muscle. This “contractile dysfunction” allows blood to become stagnant (stasis) in the atria, especially in the left atrial appendage. Stagnant blood is prone to clot formation, and a clot can break off, travel through the bloodstream, and block a cerebral artery, causing an ischemic stroke.

**Relevant medical context**  
- AF is a major cardiac cause of stroke, and the pathogenesis involves thrombus formation in patients with AF.  
- The dysrhythmia causes contractile dysfunction and stasis, which further increases the risk of thromboembolism.  
- AF is associated with a substantial increase in stroke and other thromboembolic events.

**What to watch out for**  
- The risk of stroke is linked to the degree of atrial stasis and clot formation; therefore, anticoagulation therapy is often recommended to reduce this risk.  
- Monitoring for signs of clot formation (e.g., new neurological symptoms) and managing underlying heart rhythm are important in patients with AF.

**Inference on Transparency and Accountability Mechanisms for the Central Authority**

1. **Transparency Measures**  
   - **Public Disclosure of Records** – All records related to the Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS) must be placed in the public domain and kept open for inspection by the public (National Food Security Act, § 27).  
   - **Social Audits** – Local authorities or any body authorized by the State Government must conduct periodic social audits of fair‑price shops, TPDS and other welfare schemes, publicise the findings and take necessary action (National Food Security Act, § 28). The Central Government may also commission independent agencies to carry out such audits.  
   - **Annual Financial Statements** – The Central Authority is required to prepare an annual statement of accounts in the form prescribed by the Central Government (Aadhaar Act, § 26).  

2. **Accountability Measures**  
   - **Investigation Wing** – The Central Authority has an Investigation Wing headed by a Director‑General, with appointed Additional Director‑Generals, Directors, Joint Directors, Deputy Directors and Assistant Directors who exercise powers under the general control and supervision of the Director‑General (Aadhaar Act, § 15).

   - **Protection of Good‑Faith Actions** – No suit, prosecution or legal proceeding can be instituted against the President, members, Chief Commissioner, Commissioners, officers, employees or any person acting in good faith under the Act (Aadhaar Act, § 98).

**Direct answer**  
The scheme improves nutrient‑use efficiency in districts by promoting soil‑test‑based nutrient management. It does this through:

* **Soil testing and Soil Health Cards** – every farmer receives a card that shows the status of 12 soil parameters (N, P, K, S, Zn, Fe, Cu, Mn, B, pH, EC, OC) and gives fertilizer‑recommendations tailored to the farm’s needs.  
* **Block‑level fertilizer recommendations** – standardized sampling and analysis are used to design taluka/block‑level fertilizer recommendations for targeted districts, ensuring that nutrients are applied only where they are required.  
* **Capacity building and extension** – district and state staff, as well as progressive farmers, are trained to promote balanced and integrated nutrient‑management practices.  
* **Financial assistance** – farmers receive support to apply corrective measures (e.g., micronutrients, lime) and to adopt balanced fertilizer use as advised on the Soil Health Card.  

**Action steps (as outlined in the scheme)**  

1. **Get the soil tested** – obtain a Soil Health Card for each holding (issued every two years).  
2. **Follow the card’s recommendations** – apply the suggested quantities of macro‑ and micronutrients, and any soil amendments (e.g., lime) to correct deficiencies.  
3. **Adopt balanced/integrated nutrient management** – combine organic inputs (green manuring, vermicompost) with recommended chemical fertilizers as per the card.  
4. **Utilize available financial assistance** – apply for the scheme’s support to cover the cost of corrective inputs.  

**Scheme/advisory pointers**  

* **Soil Health Card Scheme** – the core programme delivering soil‑test‑based advisories.  
* **Strengthening Soil Testing Laboratories (STLs)** – capacity‑building and linkage with ICAR/State Agricultural Universities to ensure reliable testing.  
* **Krishibhavan/Extension network** – local agricultural officers provide on‑ground guidance and monitor implementation at the panchayat and block levels.  

**Short caution note**  
Always follow the label instructions on fertilizer bags and consult your local agriculture officer or Krishi Vigyan Kendra before applying any input, especially when using new micronutrients or amendments.

The Nutrient‑Based Subsidy (NBS) scheme and the Soil Health Card (SHC) programme are complementary tools for promoting balanced fertilizer use:

* **Soil Health Card** – Provides a farmer‑specific report on the status of 12 soil parameters (macro‑nutrients N, P, K; secondary nutrient S; micro‑nutrients Zn, Fe, Cu, Mn, B; and physical parameters pH, EC, OC). Based on this analysis, the SHC gives fertilizer‑type and dosage recommendations that are tailored to the farmer’s soil condition.  
* **Nutrient‑Based Subsidy** – A subsidy policy that is applied to phosphatic (P) and potassic (K) fertilizers, i.e., it provides financial support based on the nutrient content of the fertilizer rather than on the product itself.  

Because the SHC tells a farmer exactly which nutrients (and in what amounts) are needed, the NBS subsidy encourages the farmer to purchase the recommended P‑ and K‑containing fertilizers at a reduced cost. In this way, the two schemes work together: the SHC supplies the scientific basis for nutrient management, and the NBS makes the required nutrients more affordable, helping farmers follow the balanced‑fertilizer advice given on their Soil Health Card.

**Precautions a person with pulmonary (lung) TB should take to protect others**

- **Wear a mask** – The patient should wear a surgical or mouth‑nose mask when around other people to reduce the spread of infectious droplets [1].  
- **Practice effective cough hygiene** – Cover the mouth and nose with a tissue or the elbow when coughing or sneezing, and dispose of tissues properly [2].  
- **Limit close contact** – Avoid being in close proximity to others, especially in poorly ventilated indoor spaces, until the infection is no longer considered infectious [3].  
- **Use a private or well‑ventilated area** – If possible, stay in a separate room or a space with good airflow to minimize the chance of transmitting airborne bacteria [3].  

These measures are part of standard airborne infection‑control precautions for infectious pulmonary TB.

**Relevant medical context**  
TB is caused by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* and spreads through the air when a person with active lung TB coughs, sneezes, talks, or sings. It is not spread by touching, kissing, or sharing food or dishes [4].

**What to watch out for**  
- Ensure the mask fits snugly over the nose and mouth.  
- Replace or wash masks regularly, especially if they become damp.  
- Continue cough hygiene even when wearing a mask, as masks alone are not sufficient.  

Please consult a qualified doctor for personal medical advice.

retrieved_contexts: ["Cancer Also called: Carcinoma, Malignancy, Neoplasms, Tumor On this page Basics Summary Start Here Diagnosis and Tests Prevention and Risk Factors Treatments and Therapies Learn More Living With Related Issues Specifics Genetics See, Play and Learn Videos and Tutorials Research Statistics and Research Clinical Trials Journal Articles Resources Reference Desk Find an Expert For You Children Teenagers Men Women Patient Handouts Summary What is cancer? Cancer is not just one disease but many diseases. Cancer begins in your cells, which are the building blocks of your body. Usually, your body forms new cells as needed, replacing old cells that die. Sometimes this process goes wrong. New cells grow even when you don't need them, and old cells don't die when they should. These extra cells can form a mass called a tumor. Tumors can be benign or malignant. Benign tumors aren't cancer, while malignant ones are. Cells from malignant tumors can invade nearby tissues. They can also break away and spread to other parts of your body. The spread of cancer from one part of the body to another is called metastasis. The Nutrient Based Subsidy (NBS) scheme and the Soil Health Card (SHC) programme are two complementary government initiatives aimed at improving nutrient use efficiency in Indian agriculture.  

- **NBS scheme** – Provides a subsidy on fertilizers that is linked to the nutrient content of the product (nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, etc.). **Relationship**  
The SHC provides the scientific basis (soil test results and fertilizer recommendations) that guides a farmer’s choice of fertilizers. The NBS scheme then supports the purchase of those recommended fertilizers by offering a subsidy that is tied to the nutrient composition of the product. Together, they aim to promote balanced, soil‑test‑based nutrient management, reduce indiscriminate use of urea, and improve overall soil health and crop productivity.

**Steps to protect yourself and others after exposure to a TB patient in a nursing‑home setting**

1. **Report the exposure to your employer and the local health authority**  
   - The employer should have a written infection‑control (exposure‑control) plan that identifies which staff are at risk and what tasks put them at risk.  
   - You should notify your supervisor and the health‑department so that a formal exposure record can be created.

2. **Get tested for TB infection**  
   - Contact your health‑care provider or the local/state health department and request a TB blood test or a TB skin test (PPD).  
   - Testing should be done as soon as possible after the exposure and repeated if indicated.

3. **Use appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE)**  
   - When caring for patients with infectious or suspected active TB, wear an N95 particulate respirator (or an equivalent approved respirator).  
   - Use PPE especially during high‑risk procedures such as sputum induction, intubation, or bronchoscopy.

4. **Follow environmental infection‑control measures**  
   - Ensure the patient is placed in an airborne‑infection isolation room (or a well‑ventilated area) to reduce the spread of TB germs.  
   - Maintain good ventilation and air‑exchange in patient‑care areas.

5. **Participate in periodic screening**  
   - Employers should implement a regular screening program for all staff who may be exposed to TB.  
   - If you develop symptoms (persistent cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss), seek medical evaluation promptly.

6. **If you become infected or develop active disease**  
   - Follow the treatment regimen prescribed by a qualified doctor to cure the infection and prevent further transmission.  
   - Inform close contacts so they can also be evaluated and, if needed, receive preventive therapy.

- The CDC advises contacting a health‑care provider after a possible TB exposure to obtain a TB blood test or skin test.  
- A written employee exposure‑control plan and infection‑control policy are recommended to identify at‑risk staff and tasks.  
- Personal protection with N95 respirators is required when caring for patients with infectious or suspected active TB, especially during high‑risk procedures.  
- Periodic screening programs and environmental controls (e.g., isolation rooms, ventilation) are essential to lower the risk of new TB infections among health‑care workers.

**What to watch out for**  
- Ensure that the nursing‑home has a documented infection‑control plan and that you are trained on its use.  
- Verify that appropriate respirators are available and fit‑tested for all staff who may encounter TB patients.  
- Promptly report any TB‑related symptoms to your supervisor and seek medical evaluation.

Please consult a qualified doctor for personal medical advice.

**Purpose of self‑declaration in the PM‑Kisan Scheme**

The self‑declaration is used by a farmer (or the farmer’s family) to formally state the facts that determine eligibility for the scheme – principally ownership of cultivable land and any changes to that ownership (e.g., inheritance, transfer of land). By submitting a fresh self‑declaration, the farmer provides the authorities with the necessary information to:

* Verify that the family meets the eligibility criteria (land‑holding up to the prescribed limit and not falling under any exclusion).  
* Update the beneficiary record on the PM‑Kisan portal when there is a change in ownership or when a new eligible family member (such as a spouse or minor child) becomes the cultivator.  
* Ensure that the Direct Benefit Transfer of the ₹6,000 annual instalment is made to the correct bank account and that benefits are started or stopped in line with the declared facts.

In short, the self‑declaration serves as the farmer’s own attestation of eligibility and of any changes that affect that eligibility, enabling the scheme administrators to maintain an accurate, single source of truth for benefit disbursement.

**Direct answer**  
If a complaint concerns a service, the District Commission simply admits the complaint and proceeds with the case. The special procedural steps that apply to complaints about goods (e.g., the 21‑day notice to the opposite party, sample‑taking, etc.) are not invoked for service‑related complaints.

**Key eligibility criteria**  
- The complaint must be filed under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 for a service that was provided or agreed to be provided.  
- The complainant may be the consumer who received the service, a recognized consumer association, a group of consumers with the same interest (with the Commission’s permission), or a government authority.

**Required documents**  
- The complaint must be accompanied by an affidavit and any documentary evidence supporting the claim (as per the general filing requirements of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019).

**How to apply**  
1. File the complaint with the District Commission within the jurisdiction where the opposite party resides, carries on business, or where the cause of action arises.  
2. The Commission admits the complaint.  
3. If both parties give written consent, the Commission may refer the matter for mediation within five days; otherwise, it proceeds directly to hearing based on the affidavit and documentary evidence.

**Source:** Consumer Protection Act, 2019 – Section 38 (Procedure on admission of complaint).

1. **See a health‑care provider** – Tell the doctor about your symptoms and any recent travel.

- Dengue is a viral infection transmitted by infected mosquitoes; it does not spread directly from person to person.

The three main causes of anemia are:

1. **Blood loss** – losing red blood cells faster than they are replaced (e.g., heavy menstrual bleeding, ulcers, trauma).  
2. **Lack of red blood cell production** – the body does not make enough red blood cells due to deficiencies in nutrients such as iron, folic acid, or vitamin B12, or due to bone‑marrow disorders.  
3. **High rates of red blood cell destruction** – red blood cells are broken down prematurely (hemolysis) because of inherited disorders, infections, toxins, or autoimmune conditions.

The Soil Health Management (Soil Health Card) Scheme benefits the agrarian economy by:

- Giving every farmer a detailed soil‑health report (soil card) every three years, so they know exactly which nutrients are lacking and which crops are best suited for their land.

मृदा विश्लेषण में एकरूपता यह सुनिश्चित करती है कि मृदा के गुण—जैसे बनावट, संघनन (compaction), कठोरता और रासायनिक संरचना—संपूर्ण स्थल पर सुसंगत रहें। यह सुसंगतता निम्नलिखित कारणों से आवश्यक है:

- **विश्वसनीय परीक्षण परिणाम:** जब मृदा एकसमान होती है, तो विश्लेषण के परिणाम वास्तविक स्थितियों को सटीक रूप से दर्शाते हैं, जिससे मृदा की क्षमताओं या कमियों के बारे में गलत निष्कर्षों से बचा जा सकता है।
- **संरचनात्मक अखंडता:** निर्माण कार्यों में, एकसमान संघनन और कठोरता यह सुनिश्चित करती है कि आधार (sub-base) समान रूप से भार वहन कर सके, जिससे दीर्घकालिक प्रदर्शन बना रहता है और संरचनात्मक विफलता का जोखिम कम हो जाता है।
- **कृषि उत्पादकता:** एकसमान मृदा बनावट जल प्रतिधारण (water retention), पोषक तत्वों की उपलब्धता और जड़ों के प्रवेश को निरंतर बनाए रखती है, जो स्वस्थ पौधों की वृद्धि में सहायक होती है।
- **संदूषक पहचान:** एकरूपता मृदा में सीसा (lead), आर्सेनिक (arsenic) या कैडमियम (cadmium) जैसे हानिकारक पदार्थों के समान वितरण का पता लगाने में सहायता करती है, जिससे स्वास्थ्य और पर्यावरणीय जोखिमों को कम किया जा सकता है।

मृदा के गुणों में भिन्नता होने से अप्रत्याशित व्यवहार हो सकता है—जैसे कमजोर स्थान, असमान जल निकासी, या संदूषकों का असमान प्रसार—जो किसी भी योजना की सफलता को खतरे में डाल सकते हैं।

मृदा स्वास्थ्य कार्ड (SHC) योजना भारतीय किसानों को निम्नलिखित लाभ प्रदान करती है:

* **आर्थिक लाभ**
    * यह किसानों को यह निर्णय लेने में सक्षम बनाती है कि उनकी मृदा के पोषक तत्वों की स्थिति के आधार पर कौन सी फसलें बोई जाएँ और किनसे बचा जाए, जिससे वे उन फसलों पर निवेश केंद्रित कर पाते हैं जिनसे अधिक लाभ प्राप्त होने की संभावना होती है।
    * यह प्रत्येक पोषक तत्व की सटीक मात्रा के लिए उर्वरक संबंधी अनुशंसाएँ प्रदान करती है, जिससे किसान केवल आवश्यक मात्रा का ही उपयोग कर पाते हैं। इससे उर्वरकों पर होने वाले व्यय में कमी आती है और अत्यधिक उपयोग से होने वाले नुकसान से बचाव होता है।
    * मृदा की उर्वरता में सुधार करके और इष्टतम उपज को बढ़ावा देकर, यह कार्ड प्रति हेक्टेयर उत्पादकता बढ़ाने में सहायता करता है, जिससे उच्च आय होती है।
    * यह योजना प्रत्येक तीन वर्ष में मृदा स्वास्थ्य रिकॉर्ड को अद्यतन (अपडेट) करती है, जिससे किसानों को फसल चक्र और भूमि उपयोग की योजना बनाने के लिए विश्वसनीय और वर्तमान डेटा प्राप्त होता है।

* **पर्यावरणीय लाभ**
    * यह कार्ड मृदा में पोषक तत्वों की कमी और आवश्यक मृदा सुधारों (सॉइल अमेंडमेंट्स) की पहचान करता है, जो किसानों को मृदा की उर्वरता बहाल करने और बनाए रखने के लिए निर्देशित करता है। इससे मृदा के क्षरण को रोकने में सहायता मिलती है।
    * सटीक उर्वरक उपयोग से अतिरिक्त पोषक तत्वों के बहाव (रन-ऑफ) में कमी आती है, जो जल स्रोतों के प्रदूषण को कम करता है और मृदा के स्वास्थ्य की रक्षा करता है।
    * विशेषज्ञ-निर्देशित सुधारात्मक उपायों और निरंतर मृदा परीक्षण (एक ही विश्लेषक द्वारा) को बढ़ावा देकर, यह योजना दीर्घकालिक मृदा संरक्षण और सतत कृषि पद्धतियों को प्रोत्साहित करती है।

**योजना/परामर्श संबंधी संकेतक**

* प्रत्येक किसान को हर तीन वर्ष में एक मृदा स्वास्थ्य कार्ड प्राप्त होता है, जिसमें पोषक तत्वों की स्थिति, अनुशंसित उर्वरक मात्रा और आवश्यक मृदा सुधारों का विवरण होता है।
* यह योजना सुधारात्मक उपायों को लागू करने में किसानों की सहायता के लिए विशेषज्ञों की सहायता लेती है और निरंतरता सुनिश्चित करने के लिए एक ही किसान के लिए एक ही मृदा विश्लेषक को नियुक्त करती है।
* मृदा परीक्षण प्रयोगशालाओं (स्थिर, मोबाइल, मिनी-लैब और ग्राम-स्तरीय प्रयोगशालाओं सहित) की स्थापना और सुदृढ़ीकरण इस योजना के बुनियादी ढांचे का हिस्सा हैं, जो समय पर विश्लेषण और परामर्श प्रदान करने में सक्षम बनाते हैं।

**संक्षिप्त सावधानी**

किसानों को उर्वरक लेबल पर दिए गए निर्देशों का पालन करना चाहिए और किसी भी उर्वरक या मृदा सुधार को लागू करने से पहले स्थानीय कृषि अधिकारी या कृषि विज्ञान केंद्र (KVK) से परामर्श लेना चाहिए, ताकि यह सुनिश्चित हो सके कि अनुशंसाएँ उनकी विशिष्ट मृदा और फसल की स्थितियों के अनुरूप हैं।
reference: यह योजना उर्वरक लागत (8-10 प्रतिशत की कमी) और फसल उपज (5-6 प्रतिशत की वृद्धि) में वृद्धि के माध्यम से आर्थिक लाभ प्रदान करती है, जबकि रासायनिक उर्वरक के प्रयोग में कमी लाकर पर्यावरणीय लाभ भी प्रदान करती है।

**Defence strategy for a telecom company accused of tampering with Aadhaar data**

1. **Demonstrate lack of unauthorised access**  
   - Under **Section 39** of the Aadhaar Act, only a person “not being authorised by the Authority” who tampers with data in the Central Identities Data Repository (CIDR) is punishable. The company can show that it had **explicit authorisation** from the Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI) to access or store Aadhaar‑related information, thereby negating the “unauthorised” element required for liability.

2. **Absence of intent to modify or discover information**  
   - Section 39 also requires the intent “to modify information relating to an Aadhaar number holder or discover any information thereof.” The defence can argue that any data handling was **routine, authorised, and without malicious intent**, for example, limited to authentication services as permitted under the Act.

3. **Compliance with security and confidentiality obligations**  
   - **Section 28** mandates that the Authority (and any entity handling Aadhaar data) must maintain the **security and confidentiality of information**. By producing audit logs, security certifications, and compliance reports, the company can prove it adhered to these statutory safeguards, countering allegations of tampering.

4. **No alteration of demographic or biometric data**  
   - **Section 31** prohibits alteration of demographic or biometric information. The company can present evidence that it **never altered** such data, only performed read‑only authentication or verification as allowed.

5. **Corporate liability considerations**  
   - **Section 43** addresses offences by companies. The defence can argue that the alleged act was **not committed by the company or its authorised representatives**, or that the company exercised due diligence to prevent such conduct, thereby avoiding corporate liability.

6. **Reliance on lawful agreements and regulations**  
   - The company can point to the **agreement or arrangement** entered into with the Authority under the Act (as referenced in Section 39) that governs permissible data use, showing that its actions were within the scope of that agreement.

**Key legal provisions supporting the defence**  
- **Section 39** – Penalty for tampering with data in the Central Identities Data Repository (requires unauthorised access and intent).  
- **Section 28** – Security and confidentiality of information.  
- **Section 31** – Prohibition on alteration of demographic/biometric information.  
- **Section 43** – Offences by companies (requires proof of corporate culpability).  

**Source:** Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Act, 2016.

**Cancer kya hai aur yeh body mein kaise shuru hota hai?**

Cancer ek aisi bimari hai jo body ke cells mein shuru hoti hai. Body normally naye cells banati hai jab zaroorat ho aur purane cells ko khatam kar deti hai, lekin cancer mein yeh process bigad jaata hai. Naye cells zaroorat ke bina bhi badhne lagte hain aur purane cells marne ke baad bhi nahi jaate. Isse ek mass ban jaata hai jise **tumor** kehte hain. Tumors do tarah ke ho sakte hain:

- **Benign tumors** – ye cancer nahi hote aur aas-paas ke tissues ko nahi phailte.  
- **Malignant tumors** – ye cancer hote hain; ye paas ke tissues ko invade kar sakte hain aur body ke doosre hisson mein phail sakte hain (ise metastasis kehte hain).

Cancer ek genetic disease hai, matlab ismein genes mein changes (mutations) aate hain. Ye changes parents se mil sakte hain ya lifetime ke dauran bhi ho sakte hain. Jaise-jaise umar badhti hai, body ki damaged cells ko hatane ki ability kam ho jaati hai, jisse cancer ka risk badh jaata hai.

**Relevant medical context**  
Cancer cells mein shuru hota hai, jahan uncontrolled cell growth se tumor banta hai. Malignant tumors paas ke tissues ko invade kar sakte hain aur doosre organs mein phail sakte hain. Yeh disease genetic mutations ki wajah se hoti hai, jo inherited ho sakti hain ya samay ke saath develop ho sakti hain.

**What to watch out for**  
- Ultraviolet (UV) rays ka exposure (jaise dhoop mein zyada rehna)  
- Smoking  
- Galat diet  
- Physical inactivity  

Ye factors cancer develop hone ke risk ko badha sakte hain.

Please consult a qualified doctor for personal medical advice.

जो लोग अक्सर उन देशों की यात्रा करते हैं जहाँ तपेदिक (टीबी) रोग सामान्य है, उनमें टीबी संक्रमण का जोखिम अधिक होता है क्योंकि वे बार-बार उन क्षेत्रों में जाते हैं जहाँ टीबी बैक्टीरिया से संक्रमित व्यक्ति मौजूद होते हैं। बार-बार की यात्राओं का अर्थ है संक्रामक व्यक्तियों के साथ संचयी जोखिम (cumulative exposure) में वृद्धि, जिससे टीबी के जीवाणुओं को सांस के माध्यम से अंदर लेने की संभावना बढ़ जाती है।

The Soil Health Card (SHC) links directly to fertilizer management by providing a farm‑specific report of the soil’s nutrient status (pH, organic carbon, N, P, K, S, Zn, Fe, Cu, Mn, B, EC) and a set of fertilizer recommendations. Based on this data, the SHC tells the farmer which nutrients are deficient, the exact dosage of each fertilizer to apply, and any soil amendments needed to achieve optimal yields. Using the SHC guidance encourages balanced fertilizer use (instead of only urea), reduces overall chemical fertilizer application by 8‑10 % and can raise crop yields by 5‑6 %.

**2. Action steps** (as stated in the SHC guidelines)  
- Apply the fertilizers and micro‑nutrients in the quantities and types recommended on the SHC.  
- Incorporate any suggested soil amendments (e.g., lime, organic matter) to correct pH or nutrient deficiencies.  
- Follow the dosage schedule provided on the card for each cropping season.  
- Re‑test the soil and obtain a new SHC every two years (or as per the local schedule) to keep fertilizer recommendations up‑to‑date.

**3. Scheme/advisory pointers**  
- The SHC scheme is administered by the Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers’ Welfare and is rolled out through State Agricultural Universities, ICAR, and Soil Testing Laboratories.

- Capacity‑building programs are conducted for district and state staff as well as progressive farmers to promote nutrient‑management practices based on SHC recommendations.

**What makes the Soil Health Card (SHC) Scheme unique**

- **Personalised, periodic soil report** – Every farmer receives a printed card for each holding that shows the status of **12 parameters** (N, P, K, S, Zn, Fe, Cu, Mn, B, pH, EC, OC). The card is issued **once every three years**, giving a regular, farm‑specific snapshot of soil health.  

- **Specific fertilizer and amendment advice** – Based on the 12‑parameter analysis, the SHC **prescribes the exact nutrients, their dosages, and any soil amendments** needed to achieve optimal yields. This direct recommendation on what and how much to apply is not provided by most other schemes.  

- **Continuity of the same analyst** – The scheme ensures that **the same person conducts the soil analysis for a farmer across cycles**, improving consistency and trust in the results—a feature highlighted as distinct from other government programmes where the analyst may change.  

- **Nation‑wide coverage and universal target** – The programme aims to **cover all farmers in every part of the country**, with a goal of issuing SHCs to every farmer, unlike many initiatives that are limited to specific regions or categories.  

- **Integrated support ecosystem** – Beyond the card, the scheme includes:  
  - Establishment and strengthening of **soil‑testing laboratories** (static, mobile, mini‑labs, village‑level labs).  
  - **Demonstrations, trainings, and farmer melas** (over 6 lakh demonstrations and thousands of trainings since 2015).  
  - Involvement of **Krishi Sakhis, Pasu Sakhis, and other village‑level workers** to educate farmers on correct fertilizer use.  

- **Link to crop‑selection decisions** – The SHC informs farmers **which crops are suitable** for their soil’s nutrient profile and which to avoid, enabling better crop planning.  

These elements together make the Soil Health Card Scheme stand out from other agricultural initiatives, which typically focus on input subsidies, credit, or insurance without providing a **farm‑specific, science‑based soil health diagnosis and actionable nutrient‑management plan**.
reference: The scheme is unique because it aims to assess the nutrient status of every individual farm holding in the country and provide personalized nutrient dosage recommendations, making it a comprehensive and farm-specific approach to soil management.

**प्रत्यक्ष उत्तर:**  
एक ग्राम पंचायत को राष्ट्रीय आपदा के दौरान प्रभावित आबादी को रोजगार कार्ड (जॉब कार्ड) पुनः जारी करने की आवश्यकता हो सकती है, क्योंकि आपदा के कारण रोजगार कार्ड नष्ट हो सकते हैं या खो सकते हैं और ग्रामीण परिवारों का बड़े पैमाने पर विस्थापन हो सकता है। पुनः जारी किए गए कार्ड विस्थापित परिवारों को उनके अस्थायी स्थान पर पंजीकरण करने और महात्मा गांधी राष्ट्रीय ग्रामीण रोजगार गारंटी अधिनियम (MGNREGA) के तहत कार्य प्राप्त करने की अनुमति देते हैं।

**मुख्य पात्रता मानदंड (संदर्भ के अनुसार):**  
- आपदा से प्रभावित ग्रामीण परिवारों के वयस्क सदस्य, जो बाढ़, चक्रवात, सुनामी या भूकंप के कारण विस्थापित हुए हैं, वे अपने अस्थायी स्थान पर रोजगार कार्ड के लिए पंजीकरण करा सकते हैं।  
- वे रोजगार कार्ड के पुन: पंजीकरण और पुनः जारी किए जाने का अनुरोध कर सकते हैं यदि मूल कार्ड खो गया हो या नष्ट हो गया हो।

**आवश्यक दस्तावेज़ (संदर्भ के अनुसार):**  
- वयस्क सदस्यों के नाम, आयु और पते के साथ लिखित या मौखिक आवेदन।  
- रोजगार कार्ड के पुन: पंजीकरण और पुनः जारी किए जाने के लिए आवेदन।

**आवेदन कैसे करें (संदर्भ के अनुसार):**  
- वयस्क सदस्य अपने अस्थायी स्थान पर ग्राम पंचायत या कार्यक्रम अधिकारी (प्रोग्राम ऑफिसर) से संपर्क कर सकते हैं ताकि वे पंजीकरण करा सकें और रोजगार कार्ड प्राप्त कर सकें।  
- वे उसी अधिकारी को कार्य के लिए लिखित या मौखिक आवेदन भी प्रस्तुत कर सकते हैं।

**स्रोत:** महात्मा गांधी राष्ट्रीय ग्रामीण रोजगार गारंटी अधिनियम (MGNREGA) – अनुसूची II, खंड 34(1)।

The Soil Health Card (SHC) tells a farmer the exact nutrient status of his soil (pH, organic carbon, N, P, K, secondary and micronutrients) and gives a specific fertilizer‑and‑amendment recommendation for that holding. By following the SHC’s dosage and type of inputs, the farmer can correct deficiencies, avoid over‑use of urea, and select crops that match the soil’s capacity, thereby raising yields and preserving soil health.

**Action steps** (as described in the SHC scheme)  
1. **Read the SHC report** – note the levels of the 12 parameters (N, P, K, S, Zn, Fe, Cu, Mn, B, pH, EC, OC).  
2. **Apply the recommended fertilizers** – use the exact quantities and types of NPK (and any secondary/micronutrient) suggested on the card; do not rely on urea alone.  
3. **Incorporate the indicated soil amendments** – such as lime, gypsum, or organic matter, to correct pH or other physical constraints.  
4. **Choose suitable crops** – use the SHC’s advisory to decide which crops will thrive on the current soil condition and which to avoid.  
5. **Re‑test after three years** – the SHC is issued once every three years; repeat the process to track improvements.

**Scheme/advisory pointers**  
- The SHC scheme provides a printed report for each holding every three years, containing nutrient status and fertilizer recommendations.  
- Government‑appointed experts assist farmers in implementing the corrective measures.  
- The scheme promotes balanced, integrated nutrient management and helps farmers plan future cropping patterns based on soil health.

**Short caution note**  
Always verify the SHC recommendations with your local agriculture officer or KVK before applying fertilizers, and follow the product label instructions to ensure safe and effective use.

**Land records used to identify eligible beneficiaries under PM‑KISAN**

- **Land‑revenue (revenue) records** – the existing land‑revenue administrative regime and mutation records are the primary source for confirming a farmer’s land‑holding.

- **Online availability** – The Ministry of Rural Development and State Rural Development Departments must keep their websites updated to comply with the Right to Information Act, making all scheme information publicly downloadable.

The Soil Health Card (SHC) provides a detailed report of the soil’s nutrient status (N, P, K, S, Zn, Fe, Cu, Mn, B, pH, EC, OC) and the specific fertilizer and amendment recommendations for that holding. By reviewing these parameters, a farmer can see which nutrients are deficient or excessive and match them to the nutrient requirements of different crops. The SHC therefore guides the farmer to select crops that are well‑suited to the existing soil conditions and to avoid crops that would require nutrients the soil lacks.

**Action steps (as indicated in the SHC guidance)**  
1. **Read the SHC report** – note the values for the 12 parameters and the fertilizer/amendment recommendations printed on the card.  
2. **Identify nutrient gaps** – compare the reported nutrient levels with the typical needs of candidate crops.  
3. **Choose compatible crops** – select crops whose nutrient requirements align with the soil’s strengths and plan to skip or limit crops that need nutrients the soil is deficient in.  
4. **Apply the recommended fertilizers/amendments** – follow the dosage and type of fertilizers suggested on the SHC to correct any deficiencies before sowing.

- The SHC is issued once every three years (or every two years in some cycles) under the national Soil Health Card Scheme, ensuring farmers have up‑to‑date soil information.

State Governments are responsible for implementing the Soil Health Card Scheme at the ground level. Their key responsibilities include:  

- **Sanctioning and setting up soil‑testing infrastructure** – the central government sanctions funds for new and strengthened soil‑testing laboratories, which are established by the states (e.g., 11,531 new labs and 829 strengthened labs have been sanctioned to the states).

**1. Direct answer**  
The Soil Health Card (SHC) scheme helps farmers avoid crop failures by giving them a detailed report of their soil’s nutrient status (pH, organic carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, micronutrients) and specific fertilizer‑and‑amendment recommendations. With this information, farmers can:  

- Choose crops that match the soil’s nutrient profile and avoid those that are unsuitable.  
- Apply the right type and amount of fertilizers (including micronutrients) instead of relying on a single fertilizer such as urea.  
- Reduce excess chemical fertilizer use by 8‑10 % and increase overall crop yields by 5‑6 %, thereby lowering the risk of nutrient‑related failures.  

**2. Action steps** (as indicated in the retrieved information)  
- Follow the fertilizer dosage and type recommended on the SHC.  
- Apply the suggested soil amendments (e.g., lime, gypsum) to correct pH or nutrient deficiencies.  
- Select crops that are compatible with the soil’s nutrient status and skip those that are not.  

**3. Scheme/advisory pointers** (explicitly mentioned)  
- The SHC provides a formatted report every three years, ensuring farmers have up‑to‑date soil data.  
- It includes advisory on balanced fertilizer use, micronutrient application, and soil‑management practices.  
- Government experts assist farmers in implementing the corrective measures outlined on the card.  

**4. Short caution note**  
Always follow the fertilizer label instructions and, if needed, consult your local agriculture officer or KVK for guidance on applying the recommendations safely.

The Authority’s audit reports are subject to parliamentary oversight by being laid before each House of Parliament. After the Comptroller and Auditor‑General (CAG) audits the Authority’s accounts, the Authority forwards the certified accounts together with the audit report to the Central Government. The Central Government then causes the audit report to be laid before each House of Parliament as soon as practicable after receipt.

**Key points of the oversight mechanism**  

- **Annual audit** – The Authority’s accounts are audited annually by the CAG (or a person appointed by the CAG) at intervals specified by the CAG.  
- **Rights of the CAG** – The CAG (or his appointee) has the same rights and privileges as in the audit of government accounts, including the right to demand production of books, accounts, vouchers, and other documents and to inspect any office of the Authority.  
- **Forwarding to the Central Government** – The Authority sends the certified accounts and the audit report to the Central Government.  
- **Laying before Parliament** – The Central Government, upon receiving the audit report, lays it before each House of Parliament “as soon as may be after it is received.”  

**Source:** Aadhaar Act (sections on audit and annual report).

People with prediabetes already have two key problems that set the stage for type 2 diabetes:  

1. **Worsening insulin resistance** – the body’s cells do not respond efficiently to insulin, so more insulin is needed to keep blood glucose normal.  
2. **Declining β‑cell function** – the pancreas’s insulin‑producing cells become less able to secrete enough insulin to overcome the resistance.  

When these changes continue, the pancreas can no longer compensate, and blood glucose rises into the diabetic range. The combination of insulin resistance and β‑cell dysfunction is described as a hallmark of type 2 diabetes and may be driven by glucotoxicity (high glucose levels that further impair β‑cell function).

- “Declining β‑cell function, accompanied by worsening insulin resistance, is a hallmark of type 2 diabetes and may be driven by glucotoxicity.”  
- “Hyperinsulinemia refers to an elevated level of circulating insulin (80 and 100 µU/mL), often leading to metabolic disorders such as obesity, insulin resistance, and type 2 diabetes.”  

**What to watch out for**  
- Persistent elevation of fasting or post‑prandial glucose levels despite lifestyle measures.  
- Signs that β‑cell function is deteriorating (e.g., rising HbA1c despite weight loss or increased physical activity).
